## Lua

Lua has the math, table, string and utf8 libraries, a 128 MB memory limit
and a budget of about two million instructions per chunk. Native painting
and waiting run outside that instruction budget. Keep the same runner build
when continuing a painting.

A `paint` call has 12 minutes of wall time, on either sheet. A chunk still
running at 12 minutes is stopped, and the call replies "the easel didn't
answer; `log` shows whether the chunk ran". Wall time grows with the number
of stroke calls more than with their length. In the first watercolor sitting,
on the Mac GPU at 1,056 × 704 cells, stroke calls took about 0.3 seconds
each: chunks of 1,100 to 1,300 strokes took 5 to 8 minutes, and a chunk of
about 3,900 strokes was stopped. The sheet stays as it was between chunks,
so a long pass can continue in the next chunk while its paint is still wet.

## Limits of this engine

- **One dried layer.** Every dried pass folds into a single paper
  reflectance. The engine keeps no separate glaze layers and no record of
  which pigment lies where once it has dried.
- **No blotting** and no salt. Neither call is available.
- **Pigment is not conserved while it flows.** The amount of pigment can
  drift as paint moves with the water; `balance()` reports
  `conserved=false`.
- **No sizing or tilt.** Paper kinds differ in tooth and fiber texture, and
  no call tilts the sheet or changes its sizing.
- **Fast clock.** Stages that take minutes on real paper pass in seconds
  here, so time wet work by `balance()` and scratch trials.

## Finishing

- Let the sheet dry (`balance().dry`) before the final looks; a last
  `paint` chunk can `wait` and print `balance().dry`.
- The brief's final look in normal color is a whole-sheet `look` and
  detail crops, all without `mode`, taken after the last `paint` call on the
  painting. A `paint` call on the painting after them, even one that only
  waits or prints, means taking them again. `paint` calls on the scratch
  sheet leave them standing.
- Gallery and Relief looks are extra views. The studio viewer shows the
  painting in Gallery light by default; `look` with `mode="gallery"` shows
  the same.

- Value concentration: small dark marks need 1–3 pigment units per uL; washes 0.02–0.06 per uL. Concentration, not volume, drives darkness (observed on scratch).
- Long wet rows: top up every 30–60 cells to a fixed load; single long loaded strokes empty early (observed).
- Pre-wet drop grids + many rows over large dry painted areas can flood and migrate ~100 cells beyond the strokes, drying with cauliflower edges (observed once on painting; scratch trial didn't reproduce — condition difference unknown, maybe the painting had more surrounding glazes/less absorbency or more total water). Keep pre-wet away from finished focal objects.
- Opaque light streaks (buff titanium) on dark mud = collage look; opaque lights work as thin vertical grass and boat rail (observed).
- Cadmium red over dark dried paint stays bright (observed); indian red reads salmon/chalky.
- Stacked fading rows from a crisp top line make convincing mud ridges/sandbars (observed).

**Low Water, Evening Channel**

A tidal estuary at dusk. A pale channel curves from the lit horizon down to the bottom of the sheet through mudflats, and a line of old posts runs beside it into the distance. A small red boat sits on the mud below a dark bank of marsh, and a wooded headland stands against a violet-grey sky with a band of yellow glow along the horizon. The sky was painted wet-in-wet over a light pre-wet, with soft clouds added while it was still damp. The mud is built from glazes of warm, grainy paint, with sandbars and the deep foreground laid over them, and the boat's red is the one strong colour in the picture.

**Lessons, in more detail in the journal:**
- **Darkness depends on concentration.** Small dark marks needed about 1–3 pigment units per µL of water, while broad washes needed about 0.02–0.06. How much water the brush held mattered much less.
- **Long rows need refilling.** A long wash row needs topping up every 30–60 cells; one heavily loaded stroke runs out early.
- **A pre-wet can spread far.** A grid of water drops followed by many rows over dry painted mud ran far beyond the strokes. The same recipe stayed in place on the scratch sheet and I don't know why, so I treat this as a hypothesis. For now I'd keep pre-wetting away from finished focal objects.
- **Opaque lights:** streaks of buff titanium on dark mud looked pasted on and had to be painted over. The same opaque lights worked as thin upright grass blades and for the boat's rail.
- **Red over dark:** cadmium red stays bright over dark dried paint, while indian red looked chalky and salmon-coloured.
- **Sandbars:** stacked rows that start from a crisp curved top line and fade row by row made convincing mud ridges.
